title: Checkpoint: City-States
objective: After this level you can explain how Greek city-states were organized and connected.
summary: Over a thousand independent city-states, each with its own rulers, citizens and coins, still saw themselves as one people through language, gods, Olympia and Delphi.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale: over a thousand independent cities. One people?
cards.body: Each ran its own government and minted its own coins. Yet Herodotus could still speak of all Greeks as one people. What held them together?

cards.headline: What split them, what joined them

items.label: What split them
points: Their own coins and patron gods

items.label: What joined them
points: A shared language, religion and culture

cards.headline: In their own words
cards.body: Herodotus gives us a Greek definition of being Greek. In his history, the Athenians say all Greeks share kinship in blood and speech, shrines and sacrifices, and a like way of life. Notice what’s missing: a king, a capital, a single government. Greece was a family of cities, not a country.

cards.headline: One story
cards.body: Put Chapter 2 together. Mountains helped make small, independent city-states, each with a high citadel and a busy agora. Some were ruled by a few aristocrats, some by tyrants. Citizens, by birth, voted, paid taxes and fought, while metics and slaves stood outside. Each city stamped its own coins, yet all could meet at Olympia under a truce and ask Apollo at Delphi.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 complete
learned: What held over a thousand independent city-states together as one Greek people.
Who counted as a citizen, and why metics and enslaved people stayed outsiders however long they lived there.
How Greek cities were ruled by kings, a few rich families or tyrants, and why a tyrant was not always cruel.
Why hoplites fought shoulder to shoulder, each man depending on his neighbor's shield.

questions.prompt: City-States recap: about how many Greek city-states have scholars catalogued?
questions.explanation: Scholars have catalogued 1,035 Greek city-states, out of some 1,500 in all.

questions.prompt: City-States recap: which part of a Greek town was the open meeting place and market?

options.label: The acropolis
options.rationale: That was the fortified high city.

options.label: The tripod
options.rationale: That was the Pythia’s seat at Delphi.

questions.explanation: The agora was the open space for politics, trials, worship and trade.

questions.prompt: In Herodotus, what did the Athenians say united all Greeks?

options.label: Loyalty to one king and one capital
Kinship, language, shrines and a way of life
One army and a shared treasury
A single law code for every city
options.rationale: Each polis made its own laws.

questions.explanation: Herodotus has the Athenians name shared blood and speech, shrines and sacrifices, and a like way of life.

questions.prompt: City-States recap: which pairing of sanctuary and god is right?

options.label: Olympia for Apollo, Delphi for Zeus
Olympia for Zeus, Delphi for Apollo
Olympia and Delphi both for Zeus
Olympia and Delphi both for Apollo

questions.explanation: The Games honored Zeus at Olympia; the Pythia spoke for Apollo at Delphi.

questions.prompt: City-States recap: what links the slaves of Laurium to Athens’ “owl” coins?

options.label: The owls were minted in Lydia
Slaves were paid their wages in owls
options.rationale: Slaves were property, not wage workers.

options.label: The owls were stamped with a turtle
Slaves mined the silver the owls were struck from

questions.explanation: Laurium’s silver mines used as many as 30,000 slaves, and Athens struck its owls from that silver.
